- 8 Things That Lead To Emotional Exhaustion: Kind: captions Language: en - [Narrator] Hey, Psych2Goers and welcome back to our channel. Thank you so much for all the love that you've given us. Your ongoing support has helped us make psychology and mental health more accessible to everyone. As a quick disclaimer, this video is for educational purposes only and is not designed to self-diagnose signs or symptoms of emotional exhaustion. If you can relate to any of the signs in this video, we encourage you to speak to your doctor and seek medical advice if necessary. With that said, let's continue. Do you get overwhelmed by the stresses of life? Do you wind up feeling anxious when you get stressed out like this? Experiencing some daily stress and anxiety is normal, but over time, chronic stress can take a toll on your body. Emotional exhaustion is caused by a long period of excessive stress. Whether from personal stress at home or stress related to work or school. The American Psychological Association's, David Ballard, describes burnout as, "An extended period of time "where someone experiences exhaustion "and lack of interest in things "resulting in a decline in their performance." Emotional exhaustion will differ from person to person. And it's important to note that what might be stressful for one person may be more manageable for somebody else. If you've been dealing with burnout and emotional exhaustion, understanding what your triggers are, will help you manage them. Here are eight things that can lead to emotional exhaustion. Number one, high-pressure environments. Are you dealing with parents or teachers who have high expectations? Or perhaps you're working with a boss who is too demanding. Those with demanding parents, workplaces and school environments and those who work as police officers, nurses, social workers, and teachers may be more at risk for emotional exhaustion and burnout than others. For example, medical professors in the early stages of their career show higher indicators of emotional exhaustion and burnout risk. According to a 2014 study from the Netherlands, research shows that people with high performance demands and those who are preoccupied with thoughts about work and school during leisure time are more at risk of emotional exhaustion. Two, working and studying for long hours. How many hours do you work or study a day? Working and studying long hours may have some perks in terms of financial or intellectual gain, but that does not mean that it does not impact your emotional wellbeing. If you are overworking or over studying, you're sacrificing the quality time you could have with friends and family. You also miss out on your personal hobbies and time to relax. Not having a balance can tip you towards emotional exhaustion rather than maintaining a proper study life or work-life balance. Number three, financial stress or poverty. Are you often worried about having to pay for bills, housing, running a car, and groceries and food? These are all vital needed provisions and they often don't come cheap. If you worried about money, this can be a big factor that leads you to emotional exhaustion. This is especially true if you have to work longer hours or work an extra job to make ends meet. You might be stuck feeling that you have too few personal resources such as status, money or support. Number four, living with a chronic illness, medical condition, or injury. Dealing with illness or injury can be exhausting in and of itself, especially if it hinders your daily life and ability to function as you would like to. Some conditions can have a significant physical impact on you, which can cause emotional exhaustion, especially if it's hard to manage that condition or if you have little support. Number five, perfectionism. If you're someone who strives for perfectionism then you may experience emotional exhaustion and burnout in one or more areas of your life. Numerous studies have shown the perfectionism puts you at risk for burnout because of the extreme amount of pressure you put yourself under. You may be dealing with excessive stress by taking on more than you can comfortably manage. Number six, loneliness. Are you surrounded by people in your life, but you still feel lonely? Loneliness may increase feelings of emotional exhaustion because when you don't have many close relationships you don't have anyone to share your feelings with. Research suggests that fostering social relationships may help potentially less than the harmful effects of burnout by promoting resilience and a sense of greater wellbeing. Number seven, poor self-care. Do you get enough sleep at night? Do you exercise and eat healthily? If you struggle with your personal wellbeing and self care, this can also play a factor in emotional exhaustion. For example, some reasons search links insufficient sleep with a greater risk of burnout. Excessive use of alcohol or drug use may also increase this risk, especially if you use these instead of more constructive coping techniques. And number eight, significant life changes. Have you dealt with a breakup or divorce in your life or the death of a loved one? Significant life changes can throw you into a whirlwind of emotions and situations, some of which you may never have experienced before. You may turn to harmful coping strategies, such as drugs or alcohol to deal with your high levels of stress. Periods of excessive stress can cause emotional exhaustion. So looking out for some of the symptoms can help you take steps to improve them. Lifestyle changes in stress reduction methods can help. According to one research study, people who practice mindfulness report significantly less emotional exhaustion and more job satisfaction than those who do not use mindfulness techniques. So, if I had to give you two packaging-related concepts to internalize, it would be the concepts of volume and leveraging what's already worked for others. Starting with volume, most of us will spend a ton of time building up a single title and thumbnail concept. But at least in my experience, your first idea is rarely your best idea. So, one of the best things you can do to level up your packaging is simply come up with more concepts. Personally, I try to come up with at least 30 title ideas for every video I make. And I know that that sounds like a lot, but I can usually knock it out in around 20 minutes of structured brainstorming. I'll use the first 5 minutes to brainstorm title ideas from my head. Then I'll use the next 5 minutes to look at what I like to call my model five channels, or successful channels who target a different audience from me, but who offer similar type of value as I do. And I'll see if they've used any title structures that I could apply to my own video idea. I'll use the next 5 minutes to search for outliers, other people have made on my topic, videos that have way overperformed their channel's average. And I'll see if there's any phrasing or keywords that I could use. And finally, I take my last 5 minutes to take everything I come up with so far and put it into AI to generate even more variations. By the end of this process, I'll typically have a few title ideas in there that are way better than the original I had in mind. And while ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are great for this last step, I've been finding a lot of inspiration from a new feature that was just released from my long-time partner, Sprout Studio. In fact, Sprout Studio can help with the entire title brainstorming process. After you identify your model five channels, Sprout Studio makes it very easy to add them all to one list, creating a custom feed of videos that you can look at any time for inspiration, as opposed to having to check each channel one by one. You can even adjust the filters to look only at their outlier videos, or videos above a certain view count. When it comes to searching for outlier videos outside of your model five channels, you can use the outlier tab itself, searching for your topic, adjusting the filters, and browsing the outliers surfaced directly to you. But I've recently been enjoying looking for outliers in a different way, using a new feature that I've been looking forward to for a long, long time: chat. Within Sprout Studio, I can ask the chat anything I want to help me come up with new video ideas, titles, thumbnails, outlines, and more. For example, when working through round three of my title brainstorming process, I can tell it in more detail about the video I'm working on, and ask it to show me relevant outlier videos with over 100,000 views. Sprout Studio will search through YouTube and do all the hard work for me, showing me relevant high-performing outlier videos then use to inspire titles of my own. And after brainstorming a list of titles from my head, from my model five channels, and from relevant outlier videos, I can give the full list to Sprout Studio and ask it to give me even more variations. What I love about this new development is that Sprout Studio still leverages all the powerful ultra-personalization to your channel that it used to, being able to identify and replicate your own thumbnail style, and even identifying what your audience already watches, while packaging all of that power into a new way to brainstorm that's so much more intuitive to navigate and fine-tune to your liking. If you're already a Sprout Studio member, congrats. You already have access to chat. And if you want to try it out for yourself, I'll leave a link in the video description below to try out Sprout Studio for 14 days absolutely free, which I highly recommend taking advantage of, so you too can use it to have better brainstorming sessions. And I'll leave a link to my free title brainstorming template below if you want to try out this process for for And you may notice that a decent chunk of my title brainstorming time is allotted to looking at videos that have already worked well for others. That's because if a packaging concept has already worked well for someone in the past, even if they're in a different niche from you, there is a much higher chance that some version of it will work for you, too. And this applies to thumbnails as well. Recently, I wanted to make a video that was structured around a 90-day system. So, one of the first things I did when brainstorming thumbnail concepts was look for other high-performing videos related to sharing a system, a plan, or a 90-day framework. Even though the videos were in different niches, I could notice some similarities in how the thumbnails were composed and what elements were often the main characters and supporting characters. I was able to apply those insights to my own thumbnail. The result was a video that has over performed the last nine videos before it. So, if you're in the 1K to 10K stage and you're wondering what's holding you back, chances are it's this. And if I had to go back and do it all over again, this is the area where I would spend the majority of my time improving. So, study what's already working, brainstorm more concepts, and keep iterating until you land on something that earns that much-deserved click. Now that you're getting clicks, the only thing stopping you from 10,000 subscribers is generating enough momentum. Because in order to keep growing, you need to be able to turn one great video into a second great video, and then a third, and then a fourth. And the easiest way to do that is by doubling down on what's already working for you. At this stage, you'll probably have a couple of videos that have over performed. They don't need to have gone viral in order to count. If you normally get 300 views per video, for instance, and one video gets 1,200 views, that video is an outlier. And these outliers are absolute gold mines because they signal to us that there's something in there that's attracting a wider audience. Once you've identified an outlier, the next step is to develop it into something that I like to call a video recipe, which is a repeatable content bucket comprised of a consistent audience, value, format, and vibe. We've covered audience and value already. Who are you making your videos for and what do they get out of watching your videos? Format is the structure through which you impart your value, whether it be through a vlog, a challenge, a breakdown, an interview, or something else. And vibe is the overall feeling your videos give off, which is usually determined by editing style, pacing, word choice, and environment. When those four ingredients stay consistent across your videos, your channel starts to feel cohesive. Viewers who like one video are much more likely to enjoy the next. And when this video recipe is developed from an outlier video, that's what builds momentum, effectively attracting new viewers and getting those viewers to stick around. Now, I'm not telling you to make the same video over and over again, but there should be a clear enough throughline that ties your channel together. When in doubt, a good rule of thumb to go by is the 80% rule. Ask yourself, would 80% of the people who liked your last video be interested in your next video? If not, you're probably making the wrong video. So, identify your outliers, turn them into video recipes, and keep creating within that framework. Because the clearer your recipe is, the easier it is to make consistent, repeatable content that actually grows your channel. Now, as you dial in your packaging and start doubling down on what works, it's natural for your upload frequency to take a little bit of a hit. After all, you're spending way more time brainstorming title and thumbnail concepts. You're being much more intentional about the structure of your videos, and you're probably working on improving your production quality or editing quality, as well. So, yes, it's normal to start posting a little less frequently. If you were posting twice a week, you might drop down to once a week. If you were at once a week, you could stretch to every 10 days or so, but try not to slow down too much. Because here's what tends to happen at this stage. The growth kicks in, the stakes feel higher, and suddenly there's this pressure for every video to be better than the last. And that pressure can cause a kind of creative paralysis. I've been there. Right after my channel started gaining traction, I completely freaked out and went on to make only three videos in the following 7 months. I overthought everything. I wanted every video to be a masterpiece. And I've seen the exact same thing happen to so many of my other YouTube friends at this stage. So, if that's you, know that it's normal. But if you want to break past 10K, you also need to find a way to push through it. Because momentum can only build if you keep uploading. Now, at this point, as your channel starts to grow and you start getting more visibility, something new tends to enter the picture, brand deals. And while it may feel like your big YouTuber moment, I have a potentially spicy take here, but it's a take that I do genuinely stand by. Don't take brand deals at this stage. Unless you're in a tight financial situation and really need the extra income, I genuinely recommend holding off. And I know it can feel really exciting to get your first brand deal offer because on the surface, it feels like easy money. Just mention a product and get paid for it. But in reality, brand deals are a lot of work, and they slow you way down. They make your production process longer, they add extra layers of back and forth and approval, and they can even hurt your video performance if the integration doesn't feel seamless and if it hurts retention. But more than anything, brand deals shift your focus. It's unlikely that you're going to get anything significant at this stage in your YouTube journey, and it's so much better to spend your time just trying to get to 10K through making better videos, through leveling up your packaging, or by doubling down on what works, rather than spending countless hours juggling brand scripts and deliverables for only a few hundred dollars. Now, on the flip side, there is something that I would highly recommend starting at this stage, an email list. Even if you're not sure how you'll use it yet, start collecting emails because owning your audience off platform is one of the best long-term decisions you can make as a creator. Why? Because it gives you direct access to your most invested subscribers. These are the people who want to hear from you. And if you ever want to launch something down the road, whether it's a product, a service, a course, it's so much easier to reach them through email than by hoping that a video hits their homepage. I put this off for way too long because I didn't want to give myself extra work. And yes, an email list is more effective if you're actually sending them emails, but if you're not ready for that, you can still just start collecting email addresses in the background. You can create a freebie like a checklist or a template or PDF that pairs with a video, and then offer it as a lead magnet. Or you can just put a link to sign up in your video description, or in your channel bio, or in the occasional community post. Your earliest subscribers are often your most loyal, and setting yourself up with a direct connection to them now can be huge later on. When I launched the beta version of my coaching program this year, it sold out completely, and the majority of those sales came directly through my email list. That one decision to start collecting emails was one of the biggest factors that led to a six-figure launch on a brand new offer. So, yes, first and foremost, focus on growing your channel. But as you do so, don't forget to plant the seeds of what can come next. Your future self will thank you. Once you've crossed that 10,000 subscriber mark, you've officially found something that works. You've proven that you can get attention, deliver value, and keep people coming back. Now, it's time to scale. The game from 10K to 100K is all about raising your view floor, which is the lowest number of views you get per day across your channel, regardless of whether you've uploaded that day or not. As your channel grows, that floor should rise. And the higher your view floor, the more discoverability your channel has on autopilot, and the faster you'll grow. So, how do you raise your view floor? Well, there are three main levers you can work with, producing more bangers, producing fewer flops, and increasing your quality without sacrificing quantity. Let's start with making more bangers. These are your breakout videos, the videos that bring in thousands of new subscribers and that keep performing weeks or even months after you upload them. And at this stage, creating more bangers isn't about working harder, it's about being more intentional in what you decide to make in the first place. Because when it comes to making videos that have true blow-up potential, the idea matters far more than the execution. Just take it from world-renowned YouTube consultant Paddy Galloway. I can't say it enough. Like, I'll be doing the face saying this until I think the day I die. It's like, the idea is more important than everything. So, what makes for a banger idea? In my experience, there are three main signals that can tell us if an idea has a high view potential. First, that some version of the idea has been executed before and has already gotten massive results. Second, that the topic taps into something that has broad appeal, what we'd call a high TAM, or total addressable market. And third, that the idea profoundly triggers one or more of the three click-worthy emotions, curiosity, desire, or fear. When you're trying to grow from 10K to 100K, you have to be far more discerning about what you say yes to. If a video idea doesn't meet the three major signals, then it probably shouldn't get made. Now, not every single video you make needs to go viral. I do believe that everyone should leave at least some space for experimentation and artistic expression. But if your goal is to grow, at least 80% of the videos that you make at this stage should be designed to attract a wider audience. To find those banger ideas, start ideating regularly. And I don't just mean whenever inspiration strikes. Make ideation a true habit. Some of the biggest YouTubers in the world aren't necessarily the best filmmakers, they're just the best ideators. Take Ryan Trahan, for example. Every single day, without fail, he'll brainstorm 10 new video ideas. It's a muscle that you can build. And while you don't need to write down 10 video ideas per day like Ryan, developing your own system to collect new ideas and inspiration is one of the best things that you can do. Personally, I like to take screenshots of videos that spark something in me. These videos don't need to be in my own niche. There just has to be something in the packaging or premise that makes me think, "Mhm, there's something good here." I'll drop them all into a running Notion doc and reference them whenever I sit down to brainstorm. After you develop the habit of idea generation, the real growth comes from effective idea filtration. Not every video idea you come up with is going to be a winner. So, to evaluate the quality of my ideas, I run them through a set of pretty strict criteria. Is this idea feasible to execute within my current time and resource constraints? If someone saw this video but had no idea who I was, would they still be interested in it? Would at least 80% of my existing audience want to watch this? Does this idea have the potential to hit my view goal? Is there enough proof of prior success to make me feel confident? Does this idea fit within one of my existing video recipes? If not, does it have the potential to turn into its own video recipe? Can I come up with a strong title and thumbnail for this idea? And finally, the real kicker, can I make this idea something that feels uniquely mine? Because if you truly want to make a real banger, you can't just copy someone else's idea. While proof of prior success is a powerful signal, a clone of a successful video will never perform as well as the original. So, while much of your growth up to this point may have come from studying what's worked well for others, if you really want to grow to 100K, you have to start leaning into what makes you different, what makes your videos special. For me, I realized that people responded most to the level of depth that I went into, the research, the case studies, the visuals I created to break things down. That became a part of my signature style. Once I saw that it was resonating, I made a point to double it down on it and apply it to nearly every video that I made. So, when you're evaluating an idea, don't just stop at how has this worked for someone else before? Go one step further and ask, how can I make it mine? What makes your videos different from others in your space? What do most people comment on? What do you enjoy doing that others don't? The more you lean into your unique differentiator, the harder it is to compete with you, and the more likely your videos are to stand out and blow up. With a focus on better ideas and leaning into your differentiators, you'll start to produce more bangers. But if you want to raise your view floor, you're also going to need to start producing fewer flops. Now, let's get one thing clear. No matter how good your ideas are and how much experience you have, flops will happen. So, when a video of yours inevitably underperforms, the first thing to do is ask, was this a click problem, a watch problem, or an idea problem? If it's a click problem, it means that your packaging didn't land. The title and thumbnail didn't spark enough curiosity or they weren't clear or compelling enough. In this case, you can often revise the video by reworking the packaging, whether it's new title, a new thumbnail, or both. If it's a watch problem, you need to go deeper. Pull up your retention graph and take a look at where people are dropping off. Did you lose them in the first 30 seconds or was it a steady drop throughout? Were there any particular sections that drove people away? If your average view duration is lower than it typically is, then there's something in your delivery that you can learn from. And if both your packaging and your retention look solid, it's most likely an idea problem, which means that the concept just wasn't strong enough to begin with. Maybe the TAM was too small. Maybe the idea didn't appeal to new viewers. Maybe it wasn't emotionally resonant enough. If that's the case, the best thing you can do is go back to your ideation filter and ask, what could I have added to my idea criteria that would have stopped this video from getting made? After a flop of mine that broke down how Mark Rober goes viral, I realized that it's quite difficult to generate enough interest for standalone case studies on any creator other than Mr. Beast. That realization led me to add a new filter to my ideation criteria. The more flops you have, the more specific your own ideation criteria can become. And that's a good thing, because ultimately, the goal isn't to avoid flops forever, it's to make each one count, to use them as data to build out your own internal playbook. That's how you reduce your number of misses over time and steadily increase your hit rate. As you start producing more and more bangers and fewer and fewer flops, your view floor will naturally begin to rise. And as it does so, there's one final lever to focus on if you want to scale all the way up to 100K, increasing your video quality without sacrificing your quantity. Never an easy thing to do, I know, but it's one of the biggest drivers for long-term growth. And the best way to make it happen is by reinvesting in your channel. This is the stage where you finally start accepting brand deals, not just for the extra income, but for the ability to reinvest that money into buying back your time and energy so you can create more videos without burning out. And to figure out exactly what you should be investing in, I'd highly recommend doing a time audit. Just open up a doc and list everything you do in your video creation process, literally everything. Think through the entire journey, from brainstorming to scripting, filming, editing, packaging, uploads, emails, everything. Then, for each task, estimate how long each thing normally takes you. Once you've got that down, ask yourself four questions for each task. Could this be eliminated? Does it actually need to happen? Could this be shortened or simplified? Are you overcomplicating something that could be done faster? Could this be automated? Is this something a tool could streamline? And could this be delegated? Is this something a potential hire could help with? When it comes to that last question, it can be useful to ask, in a perfect world, who would be doing this? Even if that role doesn't exist yet and even if you haven't made any hires yet, this will help you start building out an ideal vision of what your team and process could look like. For example, maybe scripting is something you love doing, so you want to keep that. But maybe editing takes forever. You realize that that's some place where you could really use some extra support. And maybe uploading is tedious and just eats up your time. Great, that's a perfect candidate for delegation. This kind of clarity gives you an exact road map of where to invest in your channel first and how to grow intentionally rather than reactively. I'll put a link to this time audit exercise in the video description below in case you want to try it out for yourself. So, whatever your elimination, simplification, automation, or delegation looks like, the goal should be to reinvest in a way that helps you create more at a higher level and with less stress. Because ultimately, this stage is all about scale. And scale doesn't come from effort alone. It comes from building up the systems to support and compound that effort. So, if you can consistently execute on smart ideas, cut back on your flops, and increase your video quality without sacrificing your quantity, it's only a matter of time before you end up with one of these. People aren't going to see your vision, but you need to be there to believe in yourself. After every video that doesn't perform as well as you hoped it would, you need to be able to tell yourself, "This video doesn't matter. The next one is going to be a banger." And then you have to repeat that to yourself as many times as it takes before it becomes true. Understand that growth is not linear. It's like planting something. Quitting smoking and alcohol can lead to significant improvements in your colon health. Both smoking and alcohol have harmful effects on the colon and stopping these habits can help your body heal. Let's first look at how smoking affects the colon. Smoking is linked to an increased risk of developing polyp, which are non-cancerous growths that can turn into cancer if not treated. It also raises the risk of rectal cancer. Smoking damages DNA and causes inflammation in the colon, creating an environment that promotes cancer development. Now, alcohol is also a major concern. Heavy drinking is a well-known risk factor for colurectal cancer. When alcohol is metabolized in the colon, it turns into acetalahhide, a toxic compound that can damage DNA. Alcohol disrupts the metabolism of folate, leading to abnormal DNA changes that can result in uncontrolled cell growth. Additionally, alcohol can alter the gut microbiome and cause inflammation, both of which increase cancer risk. So, how does quitting smoking and alcohol repair your colon? First, stopping these substances reduces exposure to harmful chemicals. This means less DNA damage in the colon cells, which lowers the chances of mutations that can lead to cancer. Second, quitting decreases inflammation. Both smoking and alcohol contribute to chronic inflammation in the colon lining. By stopping, you help restore normal tissue function and create a healthier environment that is less conducive to cancer development. Third, your body's natural repair mechanisms can work more effectively without the ongoing damage from smoking and alcohol. This means your immune system can better identify and eliminate abnormal cells that could lead to cancer. Another important factor is the gut microbiome. Alcohol can disrupt the balance of bacteria in your gut, contributing to inflammation. When you quit drinking, your microbiome can recover, which supports overall colon health. Finally, quitting smoking reduces the likelihood of developing polyp, which are precursors to colarctyl cancer. By stopping smoking, you lower your risk of these growths, further decreasing your overall cancer risk. The good news is that the risk of colarctal cancer decreases over time after quitting smoking and alcohol. However, the timeline can vary based on individual factors like how long and how much you smoked or drank. For those who drink alcohol, it is recommended to keep intake within limits of no more than 14 units per week spread out over several days with alcohol-free days included. Quitting smoking and alcohol should be part of a broader approach to colon health. This includes maintaining a healthy diet, engaging in regular exercise, and getting routine screenings for colarctal cancer. If you have a history of heavy smoking or drinking, it's a good idea to talk to your health care professional about personalized screening and prevention strategies. In summary, quitting smoking and alcohol stops ongoing damage to your colon, reduces inflammation, and allows your body to heal. This can significantly lower your risk of developing colarctyl cancer. Always remember to consult with health care professionals for personalized advice on maintaining your colon health.

- Failing at Normal: An ADHD Success Story | Jessica McCabe | TEDxBratislava: Kind: captions Language: en Translator: Leonardo Silva Reviewer: Mile Živković Hello, brains! I say that to you because, if you think about it, it wasn't really you that decided to come here today. It was your brain. And whether you decided to walk, or drive, take a taxi, or ride a bike, that decision was made by your brain. Behavior, all behavior, is affected by the brain. This is a story about my brain. So, I was a smart kid. By 18 months, I was speaking in full sentences. By third grade, I was scoring post-high school on standardized tests. I had, as all my teachers agreed, so much potential. I was also struggling. I didn't have many, any, friends outside of books. I was easily overwhelmed. I spaced out in class. I lost things constantly. And trying to get my brain to focus on anything I wasn't excited about was like trying to nail jello to the wall. But I was smart, so nobody was worried. It wasn't until middle school, when I was responsible for getting myself to classes on time and remembering to bring my own homework, that being smart wasn't enough anymore, and my grades started to suffer. My mom took me to the doctor and, after a comprehensive evaluation, I was diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, ADHD. If you're not familiar with ADHD, it has three primary characteristics: inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity. Some people with ADHD have more of the inattentive presentation. Those are the daydreamers, the space cadets. Some have more of the hyperactive-impulsive presentation. Those are the kids that usually get diagnosed early. (Laughter) But the most common presentation is a combination of both. My doctor and my parents decided that, given my shiny, new diagnosis, maybe stimulant medication would succeed where spankings and lectures had failed. So I tried it, and it worked. The first time I took my medication, it was like putting on glasses and realizing I could see without squinting. I could focus. And without changing anything, my GPA went up a full point. Honestly, it was kind of miraculous. By 14, I had friends that liked me. By 15, I had published my first poem. I got a boyfriend. By 17, I knew I wanted to be a journalist. My local college had a program that would guarantee admission to USC. They had a really great journalism program. So, I signed up at my local college and I started taking classes. I moved in with my boyfriend. Things were going great, until they weren't. I started having trouble making it to class on time. I aced a statistics course, but I forgot to sign up in time, so I never got the credit. I took classes so I could help my boyfriend with his career, but I completely lost sight of mine. I never made it to USC. By 21, I dropped out of college and moved back home. Over the next ten years, I started and quit, or was fired from, 15 jobs. I ruined my credit. I got married, and was divorced within a year. At this point, I was 32, and I had no idea what I was doing with my life, besides reading self-help books that didn't seem to be helping. What happened to all that potential? Was I not trying? No! I worked harder than anyone I knew. I didn't even have time for friends. I was that busy. I had potential, though. So, my failure was clearly my fault. I just hadn't done what I need to do to reach it, and, honestly, I was tired of trying, putting more effort into life than everyone else and falling farther and farther behind. At this point, I could have given up on myself, I could have decided that everyone who'd thought I had potential was wrong. But I didn't, because I knew that it was my behavior that had gotten me here, and behavior is affected by the brain, and my brain has ADHD. Looking at my behavior, I knew: even with medication, even as an adult, my ADHD was still interfering with my life, and what I needed to know was how and why, and, more importantly, what could I do about it. I started to do some research, and I found a lot of great information. I found a lot of bad information too, but that's another talk. But there's good information out there. Websites, podcasts, talks, by researchers and medical professionals; books that would have been way more helpful than the self-help books I'd been using that were clearly written for normal - well, there's no normal - neurotypical brains. A lot of what I found, though, was either super technical or seemed like it was written for parents and teachers trying to deal with ADHD kids. There wasn't a lot that seemed intended for us, the people who have ADHD. So, I started a YouTube channel. I had no idea how to start a YouTube channel, but I started a YouTube channel. I almost called it "How Not To ADHD," because that was about all I knew at the time. But my boyfriend, Edward, talked me out of it. It turns out lots of people need help understanding ADHD, including, maybe especially, those who actually have it. I was no exception. I thought ADHD was kind of the same for everybody. I thought it was mostly about getting distracted. I thought having ADHD was maybe the reason that I was failing at life. And I thought I was what needed to change, in order to be successful. I couldn't be successful and still be me. Spoilers: I was wrong. So, let's go back for a second, let's go back to what brought us here today: the brain. Understanding the brain you're working with, it turns out, is kind of important, and that's true whether that brain is your employee's, your student's, your kid's, your significant other's, or your own. ADHD affects between 5 and 8% of the global population, which means, statistically speaking, there's between 37 and 60 of us just in this room. You can't tell who we are just by looking, but it's fun to watch you try. So, at some point, you're going to meet someone with ADHD, work with them, give birth to them, or fall in love with them. Chances are you already have. And, at some point, you're going to ask yourself, "What is going on in their brain?!" So, after two years of learning about ADHD and a lifetime of experience with it, after having the honor of connecting with researchers, and doctors, and ADHD experts, and tens of thousands of ADHD brains all over the world, what can I tell you to help you understand ADHD? By the way, many of them helped with this talk. First of all, it's real. It's not bad parenting or lack of discipline. ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder. It's currently the most well-researched mental condition, and there are actually measurable differences in the brain. These differences are larger in children, but, for most people, they never go away. In other words, adults have ADHD too. While rates of ADHD diagnosis are increasing, it's not because of an increase in sugar or technology, or lack of spanking; it's not, any more than people drowning in swimming pools is because of Nicolas Cage. Correlation does not equal causation. Those are real numbers. It's from both an increase in understanding that ADHD exists, that girls, adults, and gifted students can have it too, and ironically a lack of understanding that being hyper, misbehaving, or struggling in school does not mean you have ADHD. ADHD is more serious than I realized. The primary characteristics - inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity - don't sound all that serious, and I didn't think that they were, but, in real life, they translate to people getting into more accidents, being more likely to get fired, get divorced, significantly more likely to struggle with addiction. I learned that ADHD is on a spectrum. Raise your hand if you've ever lost your keys, or spaced out in the middle of a lecture. If you're not raising your hand, I'm going to assume you spaced out in the middle of this one. The thing is, while everyone experiences ADHD symptoms sometimes, an actual diagnosis is based on how many of those symptoms significantly and chronically impair multiple aspects of your life. Just like you can get sad and not have depression, you can get distracted and not have ADHD. And just like you can have mild depression or severe depression, ADHD can range from mild to severe. I also learned ADHD is a terrible name for ADHD. It creates a lot of confusion. We don't have a deficit of attention! What we have trouble with is regulating our attention. As ADHD coach Brett Thornhill puts it, it's like your brain keeps switching between 30 different channels and somebody else has the remote. Sometimes we have trouble focusing at all, and other times we get stuck on a channel and can't pull ourselves away, which in real life might seem we don't want to do homework because we'd rather play video games, and short, sometimes that's the case. But the truth is there are plenty of times we want to able to focus, we try, and we just can't. Current understanding is that this difficulty has to do with the way our brains produce and metabolize neurotransmitters, like dopamine and norepinephrine. I learned ADHD is highly treatable. Stimulant medication boosts these neurotransmitters, which is why it helps us focus. It's very effective for around 80% of people with ADHD. And I learned that medication isn't enough. ADHD affects much more than our focus. It impairs executive functions like planning, prioritizing, and our ability to sustain effort toward a goal. It affects our ability to regulate our emotions, our behavior, our sleep. It's not one program in our brain that works differently; it's the whole operating system. It can affect every aspect of our lives. And there are a ton of strategies out there that can help. Cognitive behavioral therapy, coaching, even meditation or regular exercise can help make a huge difference understanding your brain. I knew I had trouble focusing, and I knew my medication helped with that. What I didn't know was that getting overwhelmed all the time had to do with poor working memory, and that making lists helps; or that the reason I ran late all the time wasn't because I didn't care, it's because ADHD'ers have a skewed sense of time, and that using a timer could teach me how long things actually take. Mostly, I expected to learn what I actually learned: that ADHD is real; addressing it is important; and medication is not enough. What I didn't expect to learn: that I wasn't alone; I had an ADHD tribe; what a difference it would make to connect with it. There are people with ADHD in every country, every culture across the globe. Yes, even in France. And this tribe is awesome. Comparing myself to people with neurotypical brains, I felt really bad about myself. Why couldn't I keep my house clean or finish a project in time, instead of waiting till the very last second? But seeing the positives in fellow ADHD brains helped me recognize and appreciate my own strengths, ones I couldn't see when I was just staring at my weaknesses, which is what I'd been doing for decades. But ADHD brains have a lot to offer the world. We tend to be generous, funny, creative. ADHD'ers are 300% more likely to start their own business. We not only think outside the box; we're often not even aware that there is a box. We may struggle when our brains aren't engaged, but ADHD brains are great at tackling tasks that are urgent, working with ideas that are new, wrestling with problems that are challenging, and dedicating themselves to projects that are of personal interest. This YouTube career I'd stumbled into was all of those things. At 32, I was divorced, miserable, and had no idea what I was doing with my life. At 33, I'd started my own business, and was connecting with ADHD experts. By now, at 34, I have a team of volunteers helping with the channel. I'm engaged to this amazing man who helps me produce the channel, works right alongside with me, is doing the slides right now - and, as we discovered, also has ADHD. I'm working on reaching out to schools so that kids don't have to wait until they're 32 to learn about their brains. And I'm doing my very first TEDx talk here with you today. (Cheers) (Applause) But wait! There's more! Wait. (Applause) That did sound like the end of the speech. I'm sorry, it's not. I'm happier and more successful than I've ever been in my life. So, what happened? How did I reach my potential? Three things: one, I learned about my brain, my ADHD brain, both on my own and by connecting with others who have it. If you judge a fish by its ability to climb a tree, it will live its whole life believing it is stupid, unless it happens to chat with another fish and realizes fish aren't great at climbing trees, and that's okay, there's plenty of ocean. Two, in learning about my brain, I found and stumbled into a job that engages it. If you spend all your time trying to get a fish to able to climb a tree, you'll never see how far it can swim. It turns out I can be me and still be successful. I just had to find my ocean. Three, I learned strategies for challenges I still face. I have no fish analogy for this one, I'm sorry. I guess I learned how to swim. Once you know what your brain's challenges are, you can find solutions to them. Once you look past the stereotypes and assumptions about people with ADHD, and dig deeper, you learn what ADHD actually is. It's not people who won't stop fidgeting, or getting distracted. It is brains that are chronically underaroused, trying to get the basic level of stimulation all brains need. It's not about procrastinating or not caring. It's having executive function deficits that make it hard to get started. And it's not people being lazy or not trying enough. It's kids and adults struggling to succeed with a brain that doesn't always want to cooperate in a society that wasn't built for them. Society is our user's manual. We learn how our brains and bodies work by watching those around us. And, when yours works differently, it can feel like you're broken. So, what I'm trying to do is reach out to these people wherever they are in the world, and tell them, "You are not weird. You are not stupid. You do not need to try harder. You are not a failed version of normal. You are different, you are beautiful, and you are not alone." If you don't ADHD yourself, chances are you know somebody who does. They're your employee, your boss, your friend, they're in this room. I hope this talk helps you understand them better. If you do have ADHD, welcome to the tribe. (Applause) (Cheers)

- The 5 Stages of Burnout [How To Recognize Them]: Kind: captions Language: en Burnout is your reaction to prolonged&nbsp; stress that leads to mental fatigue,&nbsp;&nbsp; emotional apathy, and physical exhaustion.&nbsp; While most people think of burnout as&nbsp;&nbsp; a result of too much work, it can&nbsp; also get to us outside the office. The phenomenon often unfolds in 5 stages and&nbsp; can push healthcare professionals, teachers,&nbsp;&nbsp; new parents, people with chronic conditions, and&nbsp; anyone who bites off more than they can chew,&nbsp;&nbsp; to the brink of breakdown. It&nbsp; can present itself as follows. First, the honeymoon. You feel happy, motivated,&nbsp;&nbsp; and excited about your new challenge and as&nbsp; a result, take on a lot of responsibilities. Then there is the onset of stress. The&nbsp; initial enthusiasm gets tempered by the&nbsp;&nbsp; realities of your daily routine.&nbsp; You first start feeling tired and&nbsp;&nbsp; then anxious about not being able to&nbsp; handle everything you signed up for. Slowly signs of stress begin to surface, and you&nbsp; may develop a negative tunnel vision. Your limited&nbsp;&nbsp; capacity to pay attention to other things&nbsp; in life can lead to feelings of loneliness. Chronic stress becomes your constant&nbsp; companion and even tiny new tasks&nbsp;&nbsp; can set you off in a spiral of either&nbsp; anxiety or rage. Life may now simply&nbsp;&nbsp; feel unfair and a setback can feel like&nbsp; a personal attack or a deep injustice. Eventually, you are just exhausted&nbsp; or develop psychosomatic symptoms,&nbsp;&nbsp; such as migraines or body aches. In your free&nbsp; time, you may now just want to shut down. When you eventually burnout, apathy can take&nbsp; over—in defense against chronic stress your brain&nbsp;&nbsp; just stops caring. This is why your productivity&nbsp; plummets and you may become negative or cynical. Chronic headaches, insomnia,&nbsp; complete neglect of your own needs,&nbsp;&nbsp; or the desire to just "drop out" can&nbsp; become part of your daily routine. You reach habitual burnout, when this stressful&nbsp; state becomes your new normal and you experience&nbsp;&nbsp; constant cognitive fatigue, physical problems, or&nbsp; a mood that alternates between apathy and anger. Eventually, you may feel trapped in a&nbsp; vicious cycle of despair—with no way out. A&nbsp;&nbsp; diagnosis of major depression may be the first&nbsp; turning point towards your path to recovery. To fully heal from burnout can take months or&nbsp; even years. This is why recognizing symptoms&nbsp;&nbsp; early on is important. Because then we can&nbsp; distance ourselves from the main stressor,&nbsp;&nbsp; create enough “me” time to cool down, and do&nbsp; whatever is necessary before it's too late. The psychologist Herbert Freudenberger&nbsp; who coined the term, originally described&nbsp;&nbsp; the phenomenon as unfolding in 12 stages,&nbsp; but over time they were simplified to just&nbsp;&nbsp; five. He defined burnout as “fatigue that&nbsp; comes from caring too much, for too long”. What about you? Have you ever experienced&nbsp; any of the stages described in the video?&nbsp;&nbsp; If so, how did you recognize them&nbsp; and what did you do to overcome&nbsp;&nbsp; burnout? The main goal this week is to get your body used to fasting and protect your muscle while burning fat. In week three and four, it gets more intense. You'll do two to three fasting days per week, each one lasting 24 hours, and keep eating low carb high protein meals. You can add small portions of foods like pumpkin, berries, or sweet potato, especially after workouts, but overall it stays low carb. After the four weeks, most people continue fasting twice a week. One full fast and one shorter one, like maybe 14 to 16-hour fast to maintain their results. Overall, the diet focuses on protein, veggies, and gut health while avoiding sugar, flour, processed foods, alcohol, and most dairy. The idea is to switch your metabolism from using carbs for energy to burning stored fat instead. That's why it's called the switch-on diet. But keep in mind, it's really strict, especially in the beginning, and it's not meant for everyone. You might feel tired or get headaches while adjusting. And if you have any medical conditions, you should always check with a doctor first. So, yeah, that's the viral Korean switch on diet in the simplest way possible. What we do to our bodies makes a big difference to how we feel. Physical activity, diet, alcohol, smoking and drugs can all affect our mental health and wellbeing in different ways. So, let’s talk about them. Physical activity releases feel-good hormones called endorphins, which help us sleep and feel better. It also improves our physical fitness, which tends to make people feel better in general. Even small amounts of regular physical activity, can improve your mental wellbeing - especially if it’s doing something you enjoy. Physical activity is even a recommended treatment for some types of depression. You can get active at your own pace, in your own way. There’s no need to join a gym or even spend any money. Simple, small changes in our day-to-day can make all the difference. Taking a brisk walk at lunchtime or walking to get where we’re going, getting active in the garden, or cycling once or twice a week are great options. Ideally, we should aim to eat a healthy balanced diet, with plenty of fruit and veg. It’s important to keep an eye on your calories, and minimise foods that are high in sugar, fat and salt. - Mastering Medical Billing for Niche Practices | Avoid These Mistakes! #HealthcareFinance: Kind: captions Language: en-US Welcome to the Dr. Cham channel, Care Beyond Compare. In today's video, we'll be exploring the complexities of medical billing in specialized practices. If you're running a niche medical practice, whether it's dermatology, orthopedics, or behavioral health, you already know that billing isn't just about submitting claims and waiting for payments. Each specialty comes with its own unique challenges. From tricky coding rules to insurance quirks that can make getting paid feel like an uphill battle to help you navigate the complexities, we've gathered expert insights on the latest trends, common pitfalls, and professional tips to make your billing process smoother and more efficient. Different specialties mean different billing hurdles. In dermatology, coding can get complicated fast, especially with procedures like lesion removals or biopsies. Up coding, which means accidentally making a procedure sound more complex than it is, or undercoding, which means not capturing everything that was done, can lead to claim denials or compliance issues. Orthopedic practices face the challenge of global billing periods where surgeries often include pre-operative care, the procedure itself, and post-operative care all bundled into a single payment. Knowing when to bill separately for services is key to avoiding lost revenue. Behavioral health providers, on the other hand, often struggle with insurance coverage inconsistencies and high denial rates. Different insurance companies have different rules and without proper verification and documentation providers risk spending hours on appeals and still not getting paid. One of the biggest reasons claims get delayed or denied is incorrect coding. Specialized procedures require precise current procedural terminology and international classification of diseases codes and using outdated or incorrect codes can result in frustrating setbacks. To streamline workflows, practices should ensure their billing systems account for specialized equipment and treatment costs upfront, preventing unnecessary revenue losses. Additionally, every insurance company has its own set of rules, making it crucial to stay updated on policy changes. Insurance providers frequently adjust their coverage policies, especially for specialty services. So, keeping track of these updates helps avoid extra work for claims that will not be reimbursed. Establishing relationships with payer representatives can also make resolving denials and disputes much easier. Technology, particularly artificial intelligence, is playing a growing role in simplifying medical billing. Artificial intelligence powered tools like automated scribes and ambient clinical listening software are helping practices generate clinical notes, assign the correct codes and reduce billing errors while cutting down on administrative work. The result is fewer denied claims and faster reimbursements, making artificial intelligence an invaluable tool for improving revenue cycle management. Medical billing for specialized practices does not have to be a nightmare. By staying on top of coding rules, optimizing workflows, and leveraging artificial intelligence, health care providers can avoid common pitfalls and ensure they get paid what they deserve without the headache.
